summary: RiskyToken: ERC-20 token on Local development chain (anvil). Analysed from verified source (blockscout).
Privileged accounts can perform: arbitrary calls, minting, moving funds, blocking addresses, pausing, changing fees.
1 sensitive capability group(s) appear callable by anyone; see Permissions.
The owner (0xf39Fd6e51aad88F6F4ce6aB8827279cffFb92266) is an externally owned account: a single private key controls 9 owner-restricted permission group(s).
7 potential vulnerabilities, 7 heuristic warning(s) and 3 confirmed risky behaviour(s) detected. No finding count means a contract is safe.

findings.title: State is updated after an external call
findings.explanation: withdrawDeposit() makes an external call (msg.sender.call{…}("")) and only afterwards updates deposits. If the callee re-enters the contract before that update, it may observe stale state. This is the classic reentrancy pattern.

evidence.description: External call: msg.sender.call{…}("")
State write after the call: deposits

findings.recommendation: Confirm whether re-entry is possible and harmful. The usual fix is checks-effects-interactions (update state before calling out) or a reentrancy guard.
findings.limitations: Detected syntactically within one function body. A guard implemented elsewhere, or a trusted callee, may make this unexploitable.

findings.title: Return value of a low-level call is ignored
findings.explanation: execute(address,bytes) performs target.call(data) without checking whether it succeeded. Low-level calls do not revert on failure, so the function can continue as if the call worked.

evidence.description: Unchecked: target.call(data)

findings.recommendation: Check the boolean success value (require or explicit handling), or use a library such as OpenZeppelin Address.
findings.limitations: Silent failure may be intentional, for example best-effort notifications.

findings.title: Privileged account can make arbitrary calls from the contract
findings.explanation: execute(address,bytes) calls a caller-supplied address with caller-supplied data. This can be used to move tokens or native currency the contract holds, or to act with this contract's identity elsewhere.

evidence.description: target.call(data), guarded by modifier onlyOwner

findings.recommendation: Treat the authority holding this function as having full control. Check whether it is a multisig or timelock.
findings.limitations: This is a centralisation risk, not an external vulnerability, as long as the authority is trustworthy.

findings.title: Sensitive function without a detected access check: setFeeRecipient
findings.explanation: setFeeRecipient(address) appears to can change fees, yet UNWRAP found no modifier, msg.sender check or role check restricting it. If that is accurate, any address can call it.

evidence.description: Writes: feeRecipient; modifiers: none

findings.recommendation: Read the function body to confirm. If it is genuinely open, the value it controls can be changed by anyone.
findings.limitations: Classification relies on names of the state variables written. A variable such as `feeRecipient` set by anyone may be intended, e.g. per-user settings.

findings.title: tx.origin used for authorisation
findings.explanation: sweep(address) compares tx.origin, the original transaction sender, rather than msg.sender. If the authorised account interacts with a malicious contract, that contract can call sweep and pass this check.

evidence.description: tx.origin comparison

findings.limitations: Exploitation requires the authorised account to call an attacker-controlled contract.

findings.title: Transfers depend on settings an administrator can change
findings.explanation: The transfer path checks paused, isBlacklisted, maxTxAmount, and restricted functions can change these values. An administrator can therefore cause transfers by some or all holders to fail.

evidence.description: Transfer path conditions reference: paused, isBlacklisted, maxTxAmount
paused is written by pause()
isBlacklisted is written by setBlacklist(address,bool)
maxTxAmount is written by setMaxTxAmount(uint256)

findings.recommendation: Check the current values on-chain and who holds the administrative role before trading.
findings.limitations: This shows capability, not intent or current state. It does not by itself mean the token cannot be sold.

findings.title: Transfer fee sellFee can be changed with no detected upper limit
findings.explanation: Transfers read sellFee, and setSellFee(uint256) can change it without any detected validation of the new value. If the fee is applied as a percentage, a very high value could take most of each transfer.

evidence.description: setSellFee(uint256) writes sellFee
sellFee is read in the transfer path

findings.recommendation: Check the current fee on-chain and whether the setter is behind a timelock or multisig.
findings.limitations: Bound detection only checks whether the parameter appears in a require/if inside the setter.

findings.title: Owner powers are held by a single externally owned account
findings.explanation: The owner 0xf39Fd6e51aad88F6F4ce6aB8827279cffFb92266 has no contract code, so one private key can use every owner-only permission. If that key is lost or compromised, so are those powers.

evidence.description: owner() = 0xf39Fd6e51aad88F6F4ce6aB8827279cffFb92266; eth_getCode returned empty

findings.recommendation: Prefer contracts whose admin is a multisig or timelock.
findings.limitations: An account can delegate code under EIP-7702; this check only reflects the current state.

findings.recommendation: Check who holds these permissions (Ownership section) and whether a multisig or timelock is in front of them.

limitations: No transaction simulation was run. UNWRAP does not test whether tokens can be bought or sold.
Static analysis finds known patterns. It cannot prove a contract is safe, and the absence of findings is not evidence of safety.
Source comments and NatSpec are written by the contract author and are shown as claims, not facts.
